mcqs.question: An AST's node classes each grow a new method every time a new operation (print, type-check, code-gen) is added. What's the core problem this creates?
options: Every node class must be reopened and re-tested for each new operation, even though the operation has nothing to do with what the node fundamentally represents
AST node classes can only support a maximum of three methods each
Each operation must be implemented in a different programming language
The tree structure itself becomes invalid after the second operation is added
mcqs.explanation: The real problem is that unrelated new operations force every existing node class to be reopened and re-verified, piling up responsibilities that have nothing to do with what each node type fundamentally is. There's no method-count ceiling, no language-switching requirement, and the tree structure itself remains valid regardless of how many operations exist.

mcqs.question: In `node.accept(visitor)` calling `visitor.visitBinaryOp(this)`, what does 'double dispatch' refer to?
options: The visitor sends the same message to the node twice for reliability
The operation runs on two different threads simultaneously for performance
The node calls accept() on itself twice before returning a result
Two separate method resolutions happen in sequence: which node's accept() runs, then which visitX() method matches that node's specific type
mcqs.explanation: Double dispatch means two type-based resolutions happen back to back: first the node's actual type determines which accept() implementation runs, then that method calls the visitor's type-matched visitX() method — landing on the right node-and-operation pair without any instanceof checks. It's not about redundant messaging, threading, or calling accept() multiple times.

mcqs.question: A codebase's AST node types are fully stabilized and unlikely to grow, but new compiler passes (operations) are added every release. Which approach fits better?
options: Adding a method to every node class per operation, since it's always simpler regardless of change frequency
Visitor — it keeps the frequently-changing axis (new operations) cheap, at the cost of the rarely-changing axis (new node types) being more expensive
Neither approach works once there is more than one node type
The two approaches have identical costs in every scenario, so the choice doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: Visitor is designed exactly for this shape: a stable hierarchy with frequently added operations. It makes the common case (new operation) cheap by only requiring one new Visitor class, accepting that the rare case (new node type) becomes more expensive since every visitor needs updating. The costs are not identical, and both approaches work fine with multiple node types — it's about which axis of change is more frequent.

mcqs.question: For `visitBinaryOpNode()` to compute anything useful, it needs to read a node's `left`, `right`, and `op` fields. What does this require of the node class?
options: Nothing — visitors can read private fields directly without any exposure
Those fields (or equivalent getters) must be exposed publicly, meaning the node's internal representation becomes effectively part of its public contract
The node class must be rewritten as a set of standalone functions instead of a class
Visitor requires all fields to be stored as strings regardless of their actual type
mcqs.explanation: Visitors are external to the classes they operate on, so they can only read what's exposed publicly — meaning fields useful to any visitor effectively become part of the node's public API, trading away encapsulation for extensibility. This has nothing to do with converting classes to functions or forcing a specific field type.
